title: Bhagat Puran Singh
hook: a man who carried a disabled boy on his back for years founded the Pingalwara home in Amritsar

segments.voice: Yesterday, Amrita Pritam calling on Waris Shah, and your line was a poet mourned. Did you read about her poem? Today, someone who answered the same years with his back. Day one thousand six.

Nobody comes back for the boy. He is small, he cannot walk, and someone has left him at the gate of a gurdwara in Lahore. The man who finds him is a sevadar there, a volunteer who sweeps floors and carries water. His name is Puran Singh. He picks the boy up. Then, the story goes, he simply doesn't put him down. For years he carries the boy on his back wherever he goes: to the gurdwara, through the streets, to the library where he likes to read. When the border comes, the two of them cross it together, into a refugee camp in Amritsar.
screen: `NOBODY COMES BACK FOR HIM.` → `HE PICKS HIM UP.` → `HE DOESN'T PUT HIM DOWN.`

segments.voice: First, the boy. People who tell the story give him the name Piara, beloved. He couldn't care for himself, and nobody else would. Puran Singh had no money, no home of his own and no organization. He had a back. Second, the carrying. This is the part people remember, and it's very plain. He fed the boy, washed him, and carried him, day after day, for years. No committee decided it. No one paid him. Third, the home. In Amritsar after Partition, Puran Singh began taking in others nobody wanted: the disabled, the abandoned, the dying, people left in the streets. Out of that grew the Pingalwara, a home for them, which still cares for people in Amritsar. People began calling him Bhagat, which means devotee. Nobody appointed him; people saw how he lived. Fourth, the root. Seva, selfless service, has run through this whole path. At Ang 26 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says that it is by serving in this world that a person finds a place of honor in God's court. Puran Singh's life reads like that line acted out. Seva without a stage, without a sign on the door, with a boy's arms around his neck. That's today's line: he carried him. And the city that holds the Golden Temple's kitchen also holds the house he built.
screen: `A BOY NOBODY CAME BACK FOR.` · `CARRIED, DAY AFTER DAY.` · `PINGALWARA: A HOME FOR THE UNWANTED.` · `ANG 26: SERVE IN THIS WORLD.` · then, large: `HE CARRIED HIM.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with a load. Sit, and feel the weight of your own body on the chair or the floor. Notice your back: what it holds up, without being asked, all day. Now bring to mind one person near you who is carrying something heavy right now: an illness, a child, a debt, grief, a job that's too much. Breathe in, and feel their weight beside your own. Breathe out, and ask yourself which small corner of it you could lift today. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Pingalwara. The home for the disabled and destitute that Bhagat Puran Singh founded in Amritsar after carrying a boy on his back for years. Today's word.
Your line: he carried him. Today, carry part of someone's load: a bag, a chore, an errand, an hour of listening. Day one thousand six.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhagat Puran Singh as an example of seva, and the Pingalwara in Amritsar, the home he founded, still cares for disabled and destitute people, supported by volunteers and donors.
